s1
Imagine buying a rental, fixing it up, and getting most of your cash back out. That's the burr method. Here's how it works, with the numbers.
s2

Step one, buy. Find a house that needs work, and buy it well below what it'll be worth once it's fixed. Here the price is one hundred fifty thousand dollars. You put twenty percent down, thirty thousand, and borrow the rest.
s3
Step two, rehab. Fix it up. Here that's forty five thousand dollars of repairs, plus closing costs and about six months of holding costs. In total, you put in eighty eight thousand dollars.
s4

Step three, rent. Once it's fixed, you rent it out. At twenty one hundred a month, that's about twenty five thousand dollars a year. And the house is now worth two hundred sixty thousand, a hundred ten thousand more than you paid.
s5

Step four, refinance. Now a bank lends you seventy five percent of the new value. That's one hundred ninety five thousand dollars. It pays off your first loan, about one hundred twenty thousand, and after closing costs, you get about seventy thousand dollars back.
s6

Step five, repeat. You put in eighty eight thousand and got seventy back. Only about eighteen thousand is still in the deal, and you own sixty five thousand dollars of equity. Now you can use that same cash on the next house.
s7

But the deal still has to make money after the refinance. Here, rent minus costs and the new mortgage leaves one hundred seventy dollars a month, about two thousand a year. On eighteen thousand left in, that's an eleven point four percent cash on cash return.
s8

The big risk is the appraisal. If the house only appraises at two hundred thirty thousand, the bank lends less, and the cash left in the deal jumps from eighteen thousand to forty thousand. Always test a lower value before you buy.
